title: Commanders of Attention 1: The Attractors
coreMove: Use naturally attention-grabbing cues only when they truthfully belong to the decision.
sourcePressure: The source identifies threat, difference, and goal relevance as attractors that seize attention and shape what later persuasion can work with.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: Make the message louder, scarier, or weirder so people cannot ignore it.

hook: An abstract claim that attention changes everything
A generic meeting where someone makes a better pitch
A clever sentence about persuasion before any concrete object appears
counterintuition: You think persuasion happens during the ask, but it happens before it
The obvious factor is not always the important one
Influence is not manipulation when used well
tryThisNow: Set a timer and reflect on attention
Write down three ways to be more persuasive
Ask yourself what matters most right now

exampleSpecs.audience: a transit designer deciding how to stop track-edge crowding
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether threat can be made visible without panic
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the designer tests a sign that shows the actual train overhang at ankle height where commuters step
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a yellow platform line beside a scuffed shoe mark

exampleSpecs.audience: a QA lead warning packers about a new sesame run
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether difference from the normal label seizes attention before routine takes over
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the lead swaps in a black tray for the sesame labels so packers stop on sight before loading rolls
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a black label tray on a stainless packing table

exampleSpecs.audience: a race medic preventing heat collapse
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether goal relevance can pull runners toward salt before cramps start
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the medic places pace-band examples beside salt packets at mile eighteen, tying the cue to finishing time
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a wet pace band stuck to a paper cup

exampleSpecs.audience: a pharmacist trying to catch caregivers buying school supplies
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether a deadline cue tied to the child goal gets noticed
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the pharmacist moves the vaccine notice from the wall to the checkout bin with school forms
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a checkout bin full of sharpened pencils and health forms

exampleSpecs.audience: an incident commander waking technicians to a real risk
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether an unusual sound cue cuts through alert fatigue
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the commander plays the backup-power chirp once before the drill and asks which rack everyone checks first
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a server aisle lit by amber backup lights

exampleSpecs.audience: a fishmonger alerting staff to one dangerous lot
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether threat plus difference prevents the lot number from blending into routine inventory
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the manager places a red wax seal on only the recalled crate and asks each clerk to read the lot before opening ice
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a sealed crate sweating on crushed ice

skillTargets: identify threat, difference, and goal relevance as attractors
choose the cue family that matches the decision
reject novelty or fear when it does not belong

tryThisNowSpec: For one message, choose whether threat, difference, or goal relevance truthfully belongs in the opening cue, and delete the other two.
